title: Consent form too complex for villagers
scenario: Dr. Wanjiru Kamau leads a malaria vaccine trial in rural western Kenya. The ethics board approved a nine-page consent form, but community health workers report that many participants, most with little schooling, nod along without grasping randomisation or placebo. Enrolment must finish within three weeks or the trial misses the rainy-season transmission peak, and the funder may withdraw support. Simplifying the form further would need fresh board approval, which takes about a month. Kamau can ask the field team to use their own oral explanations that go beyond the approved text, or pause. What should she do?
options: Pause enrolment until a simplified form is approved, accepting the missed season and possible loss of funding to protect genuine understanding.
Let field staff give looser oral explanations now and file the changes retroactively, since the approved risks are unchanged and the trial could benefit many children.
Continue with the approved form but add a mandatory teach-back check, enrolling only those who can explain it, even if that slows and skews enrolment.

title: Dementia patient who once said yes
scenario: Hiroshi Tanabe, a neurologist in Osaka, enrolled a woman in a long-term imaging study when she was newly diagnosed and fully capable. She is now in moderate dementia. Her daughter, who holds proxy authority, wants her to stay in the study because her mother valued science. The next phase involves a weekly lumbar puncture, which the patient now visibly resists, pulling away and crying, though she cannot say why. The protocol permits proxy consent. Her earlier signed wish was to 'help research as long as I can.' Tanabe must decide whether to proceed.
options: Continue the lumbar punctures, honouring her earlier considered wishes and the daughter's proxy authority.
Withdraw her from the invasive phase because her present distress outweighs earlier instructions, even though this contradicts her prior stated values.
Keep her in the non-invasive imaging arm only, offering the daughter a reduced role and accepting the loss of the most valuable data.

title: A deception study and a grieving participant
scenario: Graduate researcher Luciana Ferreira is running a social psychology experiment in São Paulo in which participants are told a confederate is a fellow student, while the study actually measures reactions to staged unfair treatment. The protocol includes a debrief. During one session, a participant mentions that his brother died last month and that he is volunteering for the course credit because he cannot face anything else. He seems fragile but insists on continuing. Her supervisor is unreachable until tomorrow, and the participant's slot is now. Luciana must decide how to proceed.
options: Proceed as planned, as the participant clearly said he wants to continue and the debrief will address any distress.
Stop the session, explain the deception openly, offer credit anyway, and lose the data point plus risk a skewed sample.
Pause and offer him a choice after revealing the study involves deception, letting him decide whether to continue with full knowledge.

title: Paying prisoners for a sleep study
scenario: Warden's office staff in a Texas county jail approached sleep scientist Dr. Marcus Oyelaran, offering access to inmates for a drug-timing study. Participation would earn each inmate twenty dollars a week in commissary credit, a lot given the prison wage of cents per hour. The institutional review board, constrained by prisoner-research rules, asks him to justify the payment level. Lowering it risks recruiting too few participants; keeping it risks participants joining mainly because they are desperate. The findings may help night-shift workers, not inmates. Oyelaran must set the compensation plan.
options: Keep the twenty dollar rate, arguing that fair pay for time and burden respects inmates as workers and reduces exploitation.
Cut the payment to a nominal token and rely on those with genuine interest, accepting a smaller, slower study.
Abandon the prison site and recruit from the general community at higher cost, ensuring no coercive context.
tension: access to science vs. protection of captive populations

title: Indigenous community vetoes the genome project
scenario: Anika Johansson, a geneticist in Sweden, has partnered with a Sámi reindeer-herding community on a study of cold adaptation. Individuals consented, but the community council, after a new leadership election, now objects to any publication of the results, saying the data belongs to the collective. Sixty individual participants have not withdrawn and some are eager to see results published. A postdoc's career and a grant renewal depend on the paper. Anika must decide how to weigh individual and collective consent.
options: Honour the council's veto and shelve the paper, treating community consent as binding alongside individual consent.
Publish with participants' individual consent as the legal basis, since each person agreed and none has withdrawn.
Negotiate a restricted release, such as aggregated findings reviewed by the council, accepting a weaker paper and an uncertain timeline.

title: The surprise finding in a mapping study
scenario: Rania Haddad is a research coordinator at a Beirut university hospital where healthy volunteers undergo brain scans for a memory study. A scan of a twenty-two-year-old volunteer shows a shadow that the study radiologist thinks might be an early tumour, but she is not certain. The consent form said individual results would not be shared and the study is not clinical. The volunteer has no insurance and the hospital's own scanner is not clinically validated. Rania must decide whether to tell him.
options: Tell him promptly and refer him for a clinical scan, because the potential harm of silence outweighs the consent form's terms.
Follow the consent form and stay silent, since the study is not diagnostic and a false alarm could cause needless anguish and cost.
Ask the ethics board for an urgent ruling within days, delaying disclosure while the question is resolved formally.
tension: duty to warn vs. consent terms

title: Opt-out consent for newborn blood spots
scenario: Public health official Dr. Siobhan Gallagher in Ireland oversees a database of residual newborn blood spots. A university team wants to use them to study rare metabolic disorders, which could help families immediately. Parents were told the samples are kept for screening, with no mention of research. Re-contacting 300,000 families is expensive and would yield perhaps a third of the responses. An opt-out notice on the website would be cheap. Gallagher has to decide whether to grant access under a waiver of consent or require new consent.
options: Grant access under a waiver with a public opt-out, arguing the research is low-risk, valuable and otherwise infeasible.
Require re-contact and fresh consent, even if the sample shrinks, to honour what parents were actually told.
Approve only for anonymised, aggregate analyses and refuse any linked clinical follow-up, limiting both benefit and intrusion.

title: Adolescents and a confidential survey on safety at home
scenario: School counsellor and part-time researcher Thandiwe Mokoena runs a survey of Grade 10 learners in Soweto about household violence. Parental consent is required by the university, but she worries that sending forms home could put some students at risk or lead them to be silenced. A pilot suggests half of parents never reply, and the likeliest to reply are those least likely to have problems. The school principal supports using student assent only. Thandiwe has to decide how to obtain consent.
options: Insist on written parental consent as the rules require, accepting biased data and reduced reach to affected teens.
Request an ethics waiver of parental consent and use student assent only, protecting students from home exposure.
Use a school-wide notice with parental opt-out and anonymous responses, a middle path that still leaves some risks.

title: Selling the trial's leftover samples
scenario: Lab director Pavel Novak in Prague holds frozen tumour samples from a finished cancer trial. A biotech firm offers 400,000 euros, which would keep his lab open and fund three PhD students. The consent form allowed 'future cancer research' but didn't mention commercial use or profit. Several former patients have died; their families are unreachable. Selling could lead to a drug that helps many. Novak must decide whether to accept the offer.
options: Accept, reasoning that the research purpose matches the consent and the funds enable further beneficial science.
Decline, since patients never agreed to commercial transfer and their trust in research could be damaged.
Accept only with contractual benefit-sharing and a public disclosure, accepting that this may deter the buyer and still stretch consent.
tension: scope of consent vs. research continuity

title: Language barrier at an asylum clinic
scenario: Dr. Farid Ahmadzai runs a study on trauma symptoms among Afghan asylum seekers at a reception centre in Greece. Consent is delivered through an interpreter who happens to be a fellow resident with ties to community leaders. Some participants seem to say yes because they fear that refusing could affect their asylum case, even though the form says it will not. Farid cannot afford professional interpreters from outside. Recruitment closes this week. He must decide how to proceed.
options: Continue with the peer interpreter, stressing separation from the asylum process and trusting participants' stated willingness.
Pause until an external, independent interpreter can be found, accepting delay and possible lapse of access.
Recruit only people who contact the team directly and unprompted, keeping the numbers small but reducing perceived pressure.

title: Therapy app A/B test on distressed users
scenario: Product scientist Mei-Lin Chou at a Singapore mental wellness startup wants to test two versions of an in-app check-in. Version B is hypothesised to better retain users who report low mood, but its effect on suicidal ideation is unknown. Users agreed to terms permitting 'service improvement' but weren't told they were in an experiment. The company argues this is routine optimisation. Mei-Lin must decide whether to run the test and how to describe it.
options: Run the test under existing terms, as routine product optimisation affecting a minimal-risk interface.
Add explicit experiment notice and opt-out for all users, lowering participation and delaying results.
Run it only on users flagged low-risk and add crisis resources to both arms, accepting a biased and less informative sample.

title: Illiterate participants and a thumbprint
scenario: Field epidemiologist Esperanza Quispe is documenting parasitic infection rates in highland villages in Peru's Cusco region. Many elderly participants cannot read, and the rules require a signed form witnessed by someone literate. Villagers are suspicious of papers, recalling past land disputes, and several say they will only join if no signature is required. A local teacher offers to witness thumbprints, but participants say they fear the paper may be used against them later. Esperanza must decide how to document consent.
options: Use thumbprints with the teacher as witness, as the rules allow, explaining carefully and accepting some residual mistrust.
Switch to audio-recorded oral consent with ethics approval, which respects local norms but raises its own privacy issues.
Skip enrolling those who object to any documentation, accepting a smaller, younger sample.

title: Withdrawal after the data were pooled
scenario: Statistician Lars Eriksen manages a Danish diet-and-health cohort. A participant, Mr. Holm, writes withdrawing his data and asking for its deletion. His records were already merged into a pooled dataset that fed three published papers and an international consortium. Removing him would require re-running analyses and asking partners to delete their copies, costing several months. Holm says a family dispute makes him uneasy about his health information. Lars must decide the extent of deletion.
options: Delete Holm from every accessible dataset, ask partners to follow, and note corrections where feasible, treating withdrawal as absolute.
Remove him from future use only and leave published analyses intact, as impossible-to-reverse analysis is a reasonable limit.
Ask Holm what he is actually worried about and tailor the response, risking that conversation delays or complicates his request.
tension: right to withdraw vs. scientific record

title: Students as research subjects
scenario: Professor Gulnara Abdrakhmanova teaches an introductory economics class in Almaty and wants to test whether different exam formats affect results. Offering the experiment to all 180 students with consent would produce small, self-selected groups. Randomly assigning formats without announcing the study would give clean data and is arguably normal teaching variation. Grades count for scholarships. Some formats might disadvantage students slightly. She must decide how to proceed.
options: Randomise without telling students, treating it as routine pedagogy, and report results only in aggregate.
Seek consent and let students opt out, accepting a less rigorous design to respect their autonomy.
Run the test only on ungraded practice quizzes, removing the grade stakes but weakening relevance.
tension: power over students vs. educational improvement

title: Placebo arm in a growing outbreak
scenario: Dr. Ibrahim Sesay coordinates a trial of an experimental treatment during a haemorrhagic fever outbreak in Sierra Leone. The design includes a placebo arm, and early results suggest the drug may help, though not conclusively. Community members visiting the treatment centre are starting to demand the real drug for their relatives, and some staff threaten to leak assignments. The data safety monitoring board meets in ten days. Sesay must decide what to do before then.
options: Hold to the protocol and placebo arm until the board meets, preserving the evidence base that could help future patients.
Unblind and offer the drug to everyone now, prioritising present patients over trial completion.
Convene an emergency board meeting and halt only new placebo allocations, accepting an imperfect but quicker compromise.

title: A twin study and an unexpected paternity result
scenario: Geneticist Dr. Aoife Brannigan in Auckland is analysing DNA from a family cohort studying a hereditary heart condition. Analysis reveals that one participating father is not the biological father of his teenage son. The consent form said that individual results would not be returned unless clinically actionable, and this is not. But the son has asked to learn whether he carries the heart variant, which requires a result tied to a different paternal lineage. Brannigan must decide what to say.
options: Withhold the paternity finding and give only the clinical heart-risk result, keeping to the consent terms.
Inform the family of the finding, since the son's medical interpretation depends on accurate ancestry.
Tell the son's doctor only and leave the disclosure to them, passing along a difficult responsibility.
tension: right not to know vs. right to know

title: Compensation for a risky challenge study
scenario: Hospital ethicist Dr. Beatrix Hollander in Rotterdam is asked to review a human challenge trial in which healthy volunteers are deliberately infected with a mild flu variant to test a vaccine. The sponsor offers 4,000 euros. Many applicants are students with debt or migrants with insecure work. The sponsor says lowering the payment weakens recruitment, while raising it might make the risk too tempting. Beatrix must recommend whether to approve the amount.
options: Approve the 4,000 euros as fair pay for substantial time and risk, trusting screening and consent procedures.
Recommend capping it near lost earnings plus expenses, to avoid drawing in the financially desperate.
Approve the amount but require a cooling-off week and independent counselling before enrolment, slowing the process.

title: Photos from a village health survey
scenario: Nurse researcher Kalpana Rathod runs a nutrition survey in a remote Maharashtra district and takes photos of malnourished children to document findings. Parents gave verbal permission for the survey, but the form did not mention images. A UN-linked agency now wants the photos for a fundraising report that could bring in millions for nutrition programmes. Faces would be recognisable. Kalpana must decide whether to release the photos.
options: Release them, reasoning that the images could save many children and parents agreed to help documenting hunger.
Withhold them because the permission never covered fundraising and children's faces are identifiable.
Seek fresh, explicit parental permission and blur faces where it's refused, delaying the report and risking donor interest.
tension: donor impact vs. dignity and privacy

title: A trial participant who lied to qualify
scenario: Study nurse Obinna Eze in Lagos discovers that a participant in a hypertension drug trial concealed a kidney condition to qualify, because the stipend feeds his family. His latest labs show a worrying trend that may be related to the drug. Excluding him would remove his data and the income, and he begs to continue. The protocol requires dropping participants who misrepresented eligibility. Obinna must decide what to do before the next dose.
options: Withdraw him immediately per protocol and arrange medical follow-up, putting safety first even at the cost of his income.
Keep him in with closer monitoring, since he was candid with Obinna and withdrawing him may cause harm and shame.
Withdraw him from the drug but provide a modest hardship payment and referral, bending the sponsor's rules.

title: Covert observation in a public market
scenario: Anthropologist Dr. Tomasz Wiśniewski in Kraków plans an ethnographic study of how street vendors negotiate with tourists. Asking each person for formal consent would change behaviour and take hours. The market association approved general observation, but individual vendors have not been asked. His field notes would record physical descriptions and stalls. His university board treats public spaces as low risk, yet several vendors have complained about earlier researchers photographing them. He must decide how to gather data.
options: Observe openly without individual consent, since it's a public setting and publication will anonymise everyone.
Obtain consent from each vendor before recording anything, accepting altered behaviour and slower fieldwork.
Seek consent only from a core group of regular vendors and exclude all others from notes, narrowing but cleaning the data.

title: Experimental gene therapy for a child
scenario: Paediatric haematologist Dr. Leila Moradi in Tehran offers parents of a seven-year-old with a fatal blood disorder a place in a first-in-human gene therapy trial. The parents are desperate and eager. The child, who understands only partly, begs not to go back to hospital. Prior animal data show some benefit but also a cancer risk. The standard treatment is a donor transplant for which no match exists. Leila must decide whether to enrol the child.
options: Enrol the child with parental consent, since the alternative is death and the risk is a reasonable bet.
Delay until the child's assent is better understood and supported, prioritising his voice even at a cost in time.
Refer the family to a second independent clinician for counselling first, accepting that the delay could narrow the window.

title: Using patients' stored sera for COVID research
scenario: Pathologist Dr. Camille Dubois in Lyon holds blood from hospital patients collected for routine care, kept for months. A colleague proposes testing them for antibodies to a new variant, a project that could clarify early spread. Consent for research was never obtained and many patients have since moved or died. Ethics approval for a waiver is possible but uncertain. Dubois must choose whether to proceed.
options: Apply for a waiver and proceed once granted, since the samples are already collected and the risk is minimal.
Do nothing without consent and insist on re-contacting patients, even at a cost in time and sample loss.
Use only fully anonymised leftover samples from the legal retention pool, reducing the dataset considerably.

title: A pregnant volunteer discovered mid-trial
scenario: Clinical trial manager Dr. Yasmin Haddock runs an Australian trial of a new migraine drug that excludes pregnancy. Mid-trial, a volunteer, Ms. Parry, discovers she is pregnant but wants to continue, saying the drug is the first thing that works and she cannot afford a switch. Early animal data are reassuring but human pregnancy data do not exist. Her obstetrician is ambivalent. Yasmin must decide whether to keep her on the drug.
options: Stop the drug and withdraw her, applying the exclusion strictly to protect the foetus.
Continue under close monitoring and fresh informed consent, respecting her choice about her own body and treatment.
Switch her to open-label care outside the trial with the drug via compassionate use, separating care from research.

title: Mining workers and an exposure study
scenario: Occupational health researcher Dr. Esteban Rojas in Antofagasta is measuring silica dust exposure among contract miners. Workers agreed to the study, but the employer controls their shifts and has hinted that participants who produce unfavourable results could be marked as health risks. The union urges participation; some individual workers fear losing work. Results could prompt safer regulations. Esteban must decide how to protect participants while keeping access to the mine.
options: Give the employer only aggregated results and keep individual data confidential from them, risking denial of site access.
Share individual results with the employer to preserve access, with workers informed, since protective changes need employer buy-in.
Move to off-site testing at the union hall, losing exposure realism but removing employer leverage.

title: Consent from a fisher who cannot refuse the chief
scenario: Marine social scientist Dr. Sione Tuilagi is interviewing fishing households in a Samoan village about reef closures. Customary protocol requires the village chief's permission before anyone speaks, and the chief has instructed all households to take part. Several women privately say they would rather not discuss their catches, yet they come to the interviews. The data could influence a funding decision for the village. Sione must decide how to proceed.
options: Proceed with interviews, treating chiefly permission plus individual presence as sufficient in this cultural context.
Hold private individual consent conversations away from the chief and let people decline, even if it irritates the chief.
Use group meetings where speaking is optional and no names are recorded, balancing custom with discretion.
